affected_parts.quote: irregular brown spots on the upper leaf surface. Appearance of pale yellow trails under coffee leaf epidermis. Presence of large necrotic patches. ... Plants become defoliated and eventually die off.

summary.value: Irregular brown spots on the upper leaf surface, pale yellow trails under the leaf epidermis, and large necrotic patches caused by larval mining of the mesophyll.
summary.quote: Occurrence of irregular brown spots on the upper leaf surface. Appearance of pale yellow trails under coffee leaf epidermis. Presence of large necrotic patches.

diagnostic_features.value: Mines formed by larvae visible as pale yellow trails under the leaf epidermis, developing into large necrotic patches; larvae transparent and up to 3.5 mm in length found within mines; silk X-shaped cocoons in the axial region of the leaf.
diagnostic_features.quote: Initially, mines are formed and later develop over a large surface area leading to large necrotic patches. The larvae are present in the mines and feed on the mesophyll. ... the larvae leave the lower side of the eggs that are in contact with the upper leaf epidermis and get into the leaves. The larvae are transparent and reach 3.5 mm in length. ... Larvae leave the mines and weave a silk X-shaped cocoon, usually in the axial region of the leaf

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Coffee leaf rust, Hemileia vastatrix , was first described in 1869

type_of_disease.quote: Fungal spores germinate on the underside of the leaves and penetrate through the stoma.

affected_parts.quote: The symptoms of the disease include large orange spots on the undersides of leaves, premature leaf fall and reductions in yield as high as 80%.

summary.value: Large orange spots on the undersides of leaves, premature leaf fall, and characteristic yellow spots on the undersurface of leaves caused by spores erupting through stomata.
summary.quote: The symptoms of the disease include large orange spots on the undersides of leaves, premature leaf fall and reductions in yield as high as 80%.

diagnostic_features.value: Characteristic yellow spots on the undersurface of leaves caused by uredinia containing new spores that erupt through stomata; orange spots appear on the undersides of leaves.
diagnostic_features.quote: it eventually forms uridia that contain new spores that erupt through other stomata, causing the characteristic yellow spots on the undersurface of the leaves.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: caused by the fungal pathogen, Cercospora coffeicola

type_of_disease.quote: caused by the fungal pathogen, Cercospora coffeicola

affected_parts.quote: Small brown spots occur on the leaves, more obvious on the upper surface ... On the berries, the infections are smaller than on leaves ... in severe cases, stem dieback

summary.value: Small brown circular spots on leaves up to 15 mm diameter with light brown or grey centres, dark brown rings, and yellow margins; brown irregular spots on berries, sometimes covering the whole berry; young fruit tend to ripen prematurely.
summary.quote: Small brown spots occur on the leaves, more obvious on the upper surface ... The spots can grow up to 15 mm diameter; they have light brown or sometimes light grey centres, surrounded by a wide, dark brown ring, and a yellow margin

diagnostic_features.value: Circular spots with light brown or grey centres surrounded by a wide dark brown ring and yellow margin on leaves; on berries, spots are smaller, more irregular in shape, and mainly on the sun-exposed side; premature ripening of young fruit.
diagnostic_features.quote: Circular brown spots, mostly 5-10 mm, with bright grey centres and yellow haloes, typical of brown-eye leaf spot ... they are more irregular in shape than on the leaves, brown, and mainly on the side exposed to the sun

conflicts.note: Hawaii Coffee Ed source mentions only leaves and cherry (seed/fruit); Lucid Central also notes stem dieback in severe cases.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Black rot is caused by the fungus Koleroga noxia (also referred to as Corticium koleroga or Pellicularia koleroga in older literature)

type_of_disease.quote: Black rot disease is one of the most destructive fungal diseases affecting coffee plantations

affected_parts.quote: attacks all aerial parts of the coffee plant — leaves, twigs, branches, and berries — but not the roots

summary.value: Dark brown or black decaying leaves, twigs, and berries; dead leaves and berries remain attached to branches held by white web-like fungal mycelial threads visible on twigs and petioles; sclerotia visible over affected areas; defoliation and fruit drop occur.
summary.quote: Small dark spots form on leaf surfaces — usually near the margins or along the midrib where water tends to collect. These spots enlarge rapidly and turn jet black, giving the disease its common name.

diagnostic_features.value: White, web-like fungal threads (mycelium) visible on twigs and petioles, holding dead leaves and berries attached to branches instead of falling; sclerotia (resting bodies) scattered over affected areas.
diagnostic_features.quote: White, web-like fungal threads become visible on twigs and petioles, holding leaves and berries in place even after they die. This is a key identifying feature: dead leaves do not fall freely but remain attached to branches, suspended by the mycelial threads of the fungus. Sclerotia (resting bodies of the fungus) can also be seen scattered over affected areas.

conflicts.note: TNAU Agritech lists the pathogen as Corticium salmonicolor, while the Agriculture Notes source identifies it as Koleroga noxia (syn. Corticium koleroga / Pellicularia koleroga). These may represent different pathogens or taxonomic confusion; no taxonomy validation was available to resolve this conflict. Koleroga noxia is used as canonical per the more detailed source.
TNAU source mentions leaves and twigs/stems but does not explicitly list berries/pods as affected parts; Agriculture Notes source explicitly includes berries.
